name: ORLO-Zig (simulation)
about: ORLO-Zig: the assembly-dynamics simulation. It compares robot counts and build paths for a 10x10 tile structure, and sizes the reaction wheels.

items.title: How the simulation works
items.alt: How the simulation works
items.body:
What it is
A Python simulation of robots building a 10x10 grid of square tiles in free space. Each tile is about 160 mm (0.160 m) on a side, so the finished array is about 1.44 m across. No ground holds the structure. When a robot moves one way, the structure turns the other way, because the total angular momentum stays zero.

How it works
1. params.py holds every physical number (masses, sizes, speed limits). No other file has its own numbers.
2. A path file sets the build order (snake, spiral, backbite and others) and the type of each tile.
3. The rail and motion files turn the path into robot positions and speeds over time, inside friction and turn-speed limits.
4. momentum_core.py tracks every moving body (robots, gantry, tiles) in 6 degrees of freedom. It finds how far the structure turns at each moment.
5. validation.py checks the results against tolerances. A run that fails a check stops with an error.
6. Search and comparison scripts run many build orders and robot counts, and rank them by build time and final tilt.
7. wheel_sizing.py finds the momentum a reaction wheel must store to hold the structure still, and compares flown wheels.

How it was built
I wrote the code with AI coding agents (Pi). Each step had a written task with acceptance criteria and a test for each criterion. More than 30 test files check the physics: momentum conservation, known analytic cases, and checks that must fail when a fault is injected.

Source code: private repository (michaelkuhl10/orlo-zig). Ask me if you want access.

items.title: A lighter tile and structure, and what changed
items.alt: A lighter tile and structure, and what changed
items.body:
What changed
The tile is now thicker (30 mm, up from 10 mm). It is mostly ABS plastic, with 8 small servo motors and 4 steel pads. The old structure weight of 65 kg was a guess based on a solid tube. That is too heavy for plastic tiles.

New numbers (first estimate)
1. Structure for the whole 100-tile stack: about 15.5 kg. It is four thin steel posts, ring frames, a base plate and small brackets.
2. Robot dry mass: about 35.5 kg, down from 85 kg. This is the structure plus the 20 kg crawler.
3. System total: about 79 kg, down from 135 kg.
4. Two-robot build: each robot carries 49 tiles. Its structure is 9.3 kg, so each robot is 29.3 kg.
5. Stack pitch (the up-and-down spacing of tiles in the magazine): 30 mm, so 100 tiles stand 3.0 m tall.

How it was sized
A hand calculation assumes a launch load of 10 g along the stack and 3 g sideways. The post margins are thin (about 1.5 to 2.2). The load case is an assumption, not a real launch vehicle.

What the simulation now uses
The simulation takes the full inertia of the robot and the tile, built from the parts, and the 30 mm stack pitch. The wheel sizing and the two-robot results on this site were re-run with these numbers. The rail plane height (23 mm) and the gantry lift (30 mm) are guesses.
The search and robustness results for the build orders were not re-run. They still use the first parameters.

What is still open
1. The servo, ABS fill and fastener masses are guesses.
2. The 20 kg crawler has no parts list.
3. The 3 m tall stack on a 0.2 m base has not been checked for tipping or stiffness.
4. The simulation still ignores the 1.5 mm offset of the tile centre of mass and the spin of the servo rotors.

Every value in the new sheet carries a status: measured, CAD, datasheet, estimate or guess. Fusion CAD data will replace the guesses.

items.title: What changed in the robot and tile inputs
items.caption: Old values against the new design sheet. The tile is lighter (0.44 kg), the stack frame drops from 65 kg to 15.5 kg, and the robot centre of mass rises from 0.023 m to 0.58 m because the frame is now part of the robot.
items.alt: Three bar charts comparing old and new masses, heights and robot centre-of-mass height.

items.title: One robot: wheel need before and after
items.caption: One robot on the outward spiral. The x and y wheel momentum need grows about 3.5 times, and the z torque need grows from 18 to 25.5 N m. The build at full speed is 45 s shorter, and the time with flown wheels hardly changes.
items.alt: Bar charts of peak wheel momentum, torque and motion time, old against new, and a time history of wheel momentum on each axis.

items.title: Two mirrored robots: before and after
items.caption: The mirrored pair still cancels yaw and pitch. Roll grew: the x wheel need rose from 1.13 to 1.80 N m s, and with no wheels the final roll is 8.1 degrees instead of 0.4. Putting the old robot centre-of-mass height back brings the roll down to 0.3 degrees.
items.alt: Four panels: in-step roll results, yaw against timing delay, motion time with one x wheel, and final roll when one input at a time is set back to its old value.

items.title: Two mirrored robots, no reaction wheels
items.caption: The same build with no wheels at all, seen from the (+x, +y, +z) corner, with the new robot and tile parameters. In step, yaw and pitch cancel, and only roll is left (peak 13 degrees, final 8 degrees). If robot B is 0.25 s late, the structure also yaws up to 15 degrees.
items.alt: Two 3D corner-view animations of two robots building a 10x10 grid with no reaction wheels, with structure axes against fixed axes and a yaw and roll plot below.

items.title: Two mirrored robots, roll and pitch wheels only
items.caption: The same build with ideal wheels on roll and pitch and no yaw wheel, seen from the (+x, +y, +z) corner, with the new robot and tile parameters. In step, the structure stays still. If robot B is 0.25 s late, the structure yaws up to 15 degrees.
items.alt: Two 3D corner-view animations of two robots building each half of a 10x10 tile grid with roll and pitch wheels, with a yaw-angle plot below.

items.title: Timing between the two robots
items.caption: Yaw cancellation against the delay of robot B, with the new parameters. The 1 degree yaw limit is reached at a delay of about 0.015 s.
items.alt: Three plots against robot B delay: peak z momentum, peak z torque and peak yaw angle with no z wheel, with a 1 degree limit line.

items.title: Wheel momentum: one robot against the mirrored pair
items.caption: Wheel momentum needed on each axis, with the new parameters. The mirrored pair cancels the y and z axes; the x axis stays.

items.title: One x wheel for the mirrored pair: mass against motion time
items.caption: Five wheels asked for, plus nine more, as the one x wheel of the mirrored pair. The BCT RW4-HT is fastest (4.0 min, 3.2 kg). The Rocket Lab RW4-0.4 is the lightest fast wheel (7.8 min, 0.75 kg). Lower left is better.
items.alt: Scatter plot of wheel mass against robot motion time on log axes for 14 reaction wheels, with the BCT RW4-HT, Rocket Lab RW4-0.4, BCT RW1, Rocket Lab RW4-12 and NanoAvionics 4RW0 outlined.
